title: An overseer who says little
sum: Ignatius greets the church of Philadelphia, which rejoices 'in the suffering of our Lord without wavering' and is 'fully convinced of his resurrection', and he greets it 'above all if they are one with the overseer and with the elders and deacons' (1:0). Then he praises the overseer he had met there: his ministry came 'not from himself or through human beings', and 'by keeping silent he can do more than those who talk emptily'. He is tuned to the commandments 'as a lyre is to its strings' (1:1-2).
The greeting already holds the letter's two concerns: the reality of Christ's suffering and resurrection, and unity around the overseer. The overseer is never named.

views.H: The verbs 'I know' (1:1) and 'I found' (3:1) show Ignatius had been at Philadelphia; Lightfoot traces his guards' road from the Lycus valley through Philadelphia and Sardis to Smyrna. Ignatius sets the overseer's silence against 'those who talk emptily' (1:1); the letter does not say who they were.
views.N: 'Not from himself or through human beings' echoes Paul's 'not from people, and not through any human being' (Galatians 1:1); 'to puff himself up' is half of Philippians 2:3, whose other half comes at 8:2.
views.C: Lightfoot reads 1:0 as saying the officers were chosen by people and then confirmed by Christ through the Spirit. Who chooses ministers, and how the offices of overseer and elder relate, are the questions of the cards at Acts 14:23, Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3.

echoes: Galatians 1:1; Philippians 2:3; Revelation 3:7-13; Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1; Acts 14:23

settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To greet the church and, in the same breath, to set the terms of the letter: the greeting is meant 'above all' for those at one with the overseer, elders and deacons.
settings.readers: The Philadelphian Christians, most of them sound in Ignatius's eyes (3:1), with a group that kept apart from the overseer (3:1-3; 7:2)

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To strengthen the overseer's standing by praising his quietness above empty talk, and to remind the church that his office came from God.
settings.readers: The church, and its overseer, whom Ignatius had met on his visit (Lightfoot on 'I know')

title: Where the shepherd is
sum: 'As children of the light of truth, run from division and from evil teachings. Where the shepherd is, follow there like sheep.' Wolves 'that seem trustworthy' take 'God's runners' captive with evil pleasure, but in the church's unity 'they will have no place' (2:1-2).

views.N: Shepherd and wolves come from Jesus's warnings (Matthew 7:15; John 10:11-16) and Paul's farewell to the elders of Ephesus (Acts 20:28-29). 'Runners' is Paul's picture of the Christian race (Galatians 5:7; 1 Corinthians 9:24).
views.C: Ignatius makes the overseer the shepherd. In the New Testament the elders shepherd the flock under 'the chief shepherd' (1 Peter 5:2-4).

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To keep the church together around its overseer and away from teachers who would split it, while praising it for having 'filtered' them out already (3:1).
settings.readers: The church at Philadelphia, which Ignatius had found sound but under pressure from teachers who kept apart (Lightfoot)

title: Not the Father's planting
sum: The false teachers are 'evil weeds, which Jesus Christ does not cultivate, because they are not the Father's planting'. Ignatius had found among the Philadelphians 'not division' but 'filtering': they had strained the teachers out (3:1). All who belong to God are with the overseer, and all who repent and come back 'will belong to God too' (3:2). 'If anyone follows a maker of splits, he does not inherit the kingdom of God' (3:3).

views.N: The weeds echo Matthew 15:13 (Lake's margin) and the parable of Matthew 13:24-30; 'filtering' is the verb family of Matthew 23:24; 3:3 borrows 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, with Paul's list of sins narrowed to one, following a splitter.
views.C: The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) reads the chapter as teaching that the church is 'a visible society' and that those who leave it 'cut themselves off from God', and as condemning 'the Protestant doctrine of private judgment'. On what makes the church one, see the card on the Ephesians book page.

title: One thanksgiving, one altar
sum: 'Be eager to use one thanksgiving. For there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup for union with his blood. There is one altar, as there is one overseer along with the council of elders and the deacons.' The one meal, the one Christ, the one altar and the one overseer belong together (4:1).

views.H: Lightfoot thinks a group at Philadelphia held its own meal apart from the overseer, as at Smyrna (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1; 8:1); the stress on 'one' answers it.
views.N: The verse is built on 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 (Lake's margin): one cup, one loaf, one body.
views.C: Catholic writers cite the verse for Christ's presence in the Eucharist (Pohle in the Catholic Encyclopedia, 1909); Lightfoot reads 'altar' of the gathered church rather than the Lord's table. See the views note at 4:1 and the cards on the Supper at John 6, Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8 and Acts 20:7.

deep.b:
Ignatius uses 'altar' (thysiastērion) three times in the letters: 'If anyone is not within the altar, he goes without God's bread' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2), here, and in To the Trallians 7. Lightfoot holds that 'It would be an anachronism to suppose that Ignatius by the "altar" here means the "Lord's table"': even Irenaeus, speaking of the eucharist, 'recognised' only a spiritual altar in heaven. He takes the altar to be the church gathered in prayer, and compares the later words of Cyprian, 'one altar and one priesthood', aimed at those who held services apart. The New Testament has 'We have an altar' (Hebrews 13:10) and Paul's contrast of 'the Lord's table' with the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21).

Read either way, the sentence ties the one meal to the one overseer: for Ignatius a thanksgiving held apart from the overseer is not the church's thanksgiving (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1).

echoes: 1 Corinthians 10:16-21; 1 Corinthians 11:20-26; Hebrews 13:10; Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To draw the church away from any separate meal and back to the one thanksgiving under the overseer.
settings.readers: Philadelphian Christians who might be drawn to a gathering apart from the overseer (Lightfoot)

title: The gospel and the prophets
sum: Ignatius pours out his love and his fear: he is 'not yet complete', but their prayer will make him complete for God, so that he may reach his 'lot', martyrdom. He takes refuge 'in the gospel as in the flesh of Jesus, and in the apostles as in the church's council of elders' (5:1). 'We love the prophets too', for they pointed to the gospel and hoped in Christ, and by believing in him they were saved (5:2).

views.H: Lightfoot thinks the praise of the prophets answers Judaizers who set the Old Testament against the gospel: 'We do not disparage the prophets any more than yourselves; only we maintain the superiority of the Gospel.' Lake thinks the prophets are Christian prophets.
views.N: 1 Peter 1:10-12 and Hebrews 11:39-40 also speak of the prophets who looked forward and were made complete with the church.
views.C: Whether 'the gospel' and 'the apostles' are writings is argued (see the note at 5:1): Westcott and others took them as the Gospels and the apostles' letters, Zahn as the message; Lightfoot leans to Zahn.

settings.what: Ignatius's love and fear; the prophets
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To ask their prayer for his martyrdom, and to show the church that loving the prophets and holding to the gospel go together, preparing for the warning of 6:1.
settings.readers: The church at Philadelphia. Lightfoot thinks the praise of the prophets answers Judaizers who set them against the gospel (6:1; 8:2); the letter does not say so

title: If anyone interprets Judaism
sum: 'If anyone interprets Judaism to you, do not listen to him. It is better to hear Christianity from a circumcised man than Judaism from an uncircumcised one.' Teachers who do not speak of Jesus Christ are 'grave markers and tombs of the dead' (6:1). The Philadelphians must run from the traps of 'the ruler of this age' (6:2). Ignatius has a clear conscience: he was a burden to no one while among them (6:3).

views.H: Lightfoot thinks the teachers were Gentile Christians who had taken up Jewish practices and argued for them from the prophets; Lake says 'it is disputed' whether they belonged with the docetists of the other letters. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on the Docetae links the two in Ignatius's day.
views.N: 'Judaism' and 'Christianity' are the words of Galatians 1:13-14 and Ignatius to the Romans 3:3. Revelation's letter to Philadelphia speaks of 'those who say they are Jews and are not' (Revelation 3:9); any link to Ignatius's opponents is Lightfoot's inference.
views.C: The line judges teachers in the church by whether they teach Christ, not by their birth. See the topic on anti-Judaism for how such passages were later used.

deep.b:
Ignatius sets two people side by side: a circumcised man who teaches 'Christianity', and an uncircumcised man who teaches 'Judaism'. The first is to be heard, the second not. So the danger at Philadelphia came from inside the church: people who were not Jews by birth were urging Jewish ways on other Christians. Lightfoot: the teachers would be 'not as Jewish Christians, but as Gentile Christians with strong Judaic tendencies', since the winning of Gentile converts by Jews and Jewish Christians 'is a patent fact'. He allows, though he thinks it 'not probable', that the uncircumcised man is the hearer, not the teacher.

What they taught is not spelled out. The letter shows they appealed to 'the archives' and argued about what 'is written' (8:2), and Ignatius answers by setting the priests below the high priest and the prophets beside the gospel (9:1-2). Magnesians 8-10 warns against living 'by Judaism' and keeping the Sabbath; whether the same views were held at Philadelphia, the letter does not say.

The sentence is about teachers in the church, not about the Jewish people. 'Judaism' here is the way of life of Galatians 1:13-14, which some Christians wanted to impose (Galatians 2:14; 6:12-13).

echoes: Galatians 1:13-14; Galatians 2:14; Galatians 6:12-15; Revelation 3:9; Matthew 23:27; 2 Corinthians 11:9

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To warn the church against anyone who 'interprets Judaism' (Lightfoot: Gentile teachers who used the prophets to urge Jewish ways of life, a reading Lake's 'it is disputed' leaves open), and to defend Ignatius's own conduct during his visit.
settings.readers: Philadelphian Christians who might hear such teaching; some at Philadelphia had criticized Ignatius's visit (6:3; 7:2), whom Lightfoot takes to be the same people

title: With God's voice
sum: Some tried to deceive Ignatius 'in the flesh', but the Spirit 'knows where it comes from and where it is going'. While he was among them he cried out 'in a loud voice, the voice of God: "Pay attention to the overseer, and to the council of elders and the deacons"' (7:1). Some suspected a human informant had told him of the division. No: 'The Spirit was preaching': 'Do nothing without the overseer. Keep your flesh as God's temple. Love union. Run from divisions. Be imitators of Jesus Christ, as he is of his Father' (7:2).

views.H: The chapter recalls a scene from the visit. Lightfoot: 'It is vain to speculate' on the deceit; 'The obscurity of the allusion is a strong testimony to the genuineness of the letter.'
views.N: John 3:8 (Lake's margin) on the Spirit; 1 Corinthians 2:10 and 14:24-25 on the Spirit who exposes secrets; Matthew 16:17 on what 'flesh and blood' did not reveal.
views.C: A prophetic word in the gathering that commands obedience to the overseer: for Ignatius the Spirit and church order do not pull apart. Whether prophecy continues in the churches is asked at Ephesians 2:20.

deep.b:
Ignatius claims that his words at Philadelphia were the Spirit's, spoken 'with the voice of God'. He was suspected of having been told about the trouble beforehand and presenting it as revelation; he denies it with an oath ('the one in whom I am in chains is my witness'). Lightfoot compares 1 Clement 59:1 for a writer who claims to speak God's words, and rejects Bunsen's idea that the 'cry' was a letter.

The Spirit's message is five short commands. The first, 'Do nothing without the overseer', is Ignatius's refrain (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1; To the Magnesians 7:1). The second, 'Keep your flesh as God's temple', is Paul's (1 Corinthians 6:19) and 2 Clement's (2 Clement 9:3). The last, 'Be imitators of Jesus Christ, as he is of his Father', echoes 1 Corinthians 11:1.

echoes: John 3:8; 1 Corinthians 2:10; 1 Corinthians 14:24-25; Matthew 16:17; 1 Corinthians 6:19; 1 Corinthians 11:1

settings.what: Ignatius's cry at Philadelphia, and the dispute over the archives
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: Looking back from Troas to Ignatius's stay at Philadelphia
settings.why: To defend what Ignatius had said during his visit as the Spirit's word, to call the divided back through repentance (8:1), and to answer those who would accept nothing they could not find in 'the archives' (8:2).
settings.readers: Those in the church who had heard Ignatius speak, those who suspected him, and those who argued with him from the archives

title: The archives
sum: Ignatius did his part 'as a man made ready for union'. Where there is division God does not live, but the Lord forgives all who repent and come back 'to the unity of God and to the council of the overseer' (8:1). Then the famous exchange: 'Unless I find it in the archives, I do not believe it in the gospel.' He answered, 'It is written'; they replied, 'That is the question.' 'But to me Jesus Christ is the archives': his cross, death and resurrection, and the faith through him, are 'the archives no one can tamper with' (8:2).
readings: Read with Lightfoot (the Plain English Translation)

'Unless I find it in the archives, I do not believe it in the gospel': whatever the gospel says must first be found in 'the archives', the Jewish Scriptures. Ignatius argued from the Scriptures ('It is written'), they disputed his reading ('That is the question'), and he appealed past the argument to Christ himself.

'If I find it not in the charters,—in the Gospel I do not believe': the common reading, which Lightfoot says is 'almost universally taken', with the 'very rare construction' of Mark 1:15. The objectors refuse to believe in the gospel unless the Old Testament confirms it. Lightfoot argues against it from the parallel of the clauses.

Lightfoot reports Zahn's view, after Holsten: 'Unless I find it in the archives, that is, in the Gospel', so that the opponents appealed to original documents of the gospel. Lightfoot rejects it: 'the Greek order and parallelism are strongly against this mode of breaking up the sentence', and such an appeal would be 'an anachronism'. Lake's second punctuation sets the two side by side in the same way.

views.H: Lightfoot: the Judaizers 'pleaded the ancient charters (τὰ ἀρχεῖα) against the Gospel', in a dispute 'apparently held at Philadelphia'. The Greek word means a record office and its documents.
views.N: Ignatius's 'It is written' is the formula Jesus and the apostles use for the Old Testament. The question of how the Scriptures speak of a Messiah who suffers and rises is the question of Luke 24:25-27, 44-46 and Acts 17:2-3.
views.C: No church document discussing this verse was opened for these notes. The cards at Matthew 15, 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and 1 Timothy 3:15 give each church's teaching on Scripture and tradition.

deep.b:
The objectors' words are ean mē en tois archeiois heurō en tō euangeliō ou pisteuō. Ancient Greek was written without punctuation, and the sentence can be divided in three ways. (1) 'Unless I find it in the archives, I do not believe it in the gospel': whatever the gospel says must first be found in the archives. Lightfoot argues for this: 'The parallelism demands this.' (2) 'Unless I find it in the archives, I do not believe in the gospel', with the rare construction of Mark 1:15. Lightfoot says this is how the passage is 'almost universally taken', and it is the reading Lake prefers ('If I find it not in the charters,—in the Gospel I do not believe'), 'on the ground that "the charters" probably means the Old Testament'. (3) 'Unless I find it in the archives, in the gospel, I do not believe': Zahn's reading, which Lightfoot rejects; Lake's second punctuation has the same shape.

The Plain English Translation follows (1), Lightfoot's construction, for his reasons: the parallel of the clauses, and the rarity of the construction (2) needs. The long recension and the Armenian, which read 'I do not believe the gospel', show that some early readers took it as (2). Lake's reason, that 'the archives' are the Old Testament, fits (1) as well as (2).

Two manuscript differences touch the verse: the Greek manuscript G, with the Latin and Armenian, reads 'the ancient (writings)' for 'the archives' the first time, and the long recension reads 'I do not believe the gospel'. See the variants.

deep.h: 'It is written' and 'That is the question'
deep.b:
Lightfoot: Ignatius's 'It is written' points 'to the Old Testament Scriptures', 'according to the common use of γέγραπται in the N. T.'; he 'meets these objectors on their own ground'. Their answer, prokeitai, means 'This is the question before us, this remains to be proved'. What the dispute was about, Lightfoot infers from Ignatius's answer, the cross, death and resurrection: whether the Scriptures show that the Messiah must suffer and rise (Acts 26:23), and, against docetists, that he was truly born and died.

Ignatius then steps outside the debate: 'to me Jesus Christ is the archives'. Lightfoot: 'Though I have condescended to argue ... yet to myself such an appeal is superfluous: Jesus Christ is the archives.'

echoes: Luke 24:25-27; Luke 24:44-46; Acts 17:2-3; Acts 26:22-23; John 5:39-40; Philippians 2:3; Ephesians 4:20

title: The door of the Father
sum: 'The priests are good too, but better is the high priest', entrusted with the most holy place and God's hidden things. 'He himself is the Father's door', through which Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the prophets, the apostles and the church come in (9:1). The gospel has 'something special': 'the coming of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, his suffering and the resurrection'. The prophets pointed to him, 'but the gospel is the completion of incorruption' (9:2).

views.H: Lightfoot reads the chapter as a concession to the Judaizers ('The priests are good too') followed by the claim of something better, and the long recension as rewriting it to speak of bishops and presbyters.
views.N: Christ as high priest is the theme of Hebrews (4:14; 7:26-28; 9:7-12); Lightfoot thinks Ignatius knew the letter. 'The Father's door' takes up John 10:9 and the open door promised to this church (Revelation 3:8).
views.C: Here 'high priest' is Christ, and the 'priests' those of Israel (Lightfoot). On priests in the church today see the cards at Hebrews 7 and 1 Peter 2.

echoes: Hebrews 4:14; Hebrews 7:26-28; Hebrews 9:3-12; John 10:7-9; John 14:6; Revelation 3:8; 2 Timothy 1:10

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To honor the priests and the prophets while placing Christ above them (Lightfoot reads this as a concession to Judaizers who exalted them), and to name what the gospel alone has: Christ's coming, suffering and resurrection.
settings.readers: Philadelphian Christians who had heard the teachers of 6:1 and 8:2

title: An envoy to Antioch
sum: News has reached Ignatius that the church at Antioch in Syria is at peace. The Philadelphians should 'elect a deacon to be an envoy of God there', to rejoice with the church at Antioch and give glory to the Name (10:1). It is not beyond them: 'the nearest churches have sent overseers, and others elders and deacons' (10:2).

views.H: Lightfoot: the news reached Ignatius after he left Smyrna, perhaps brought by Philo and Rheus Agathopus, and all three letters from Troas ask for envoys (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2; Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2).
views.N: Churches sending delegates chosen by vote: 2 Corinthians 8:19-23; Acts 15:22.
views.C: The whole church elects its envoy (the verb of Acts 14:23 and 2 Corinthians 8:19). See the card on who chooses ministers at Acts 14:23.

echoes: 2 Corinthians 8:19-23; Acts 14:23; Acts 15:22; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2; Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To bring the churches of Asia into fellowship with the church at Antioch now that its trouble had ended, and so to secure Ignatius's own church after he was gone (Lake's third motive: 'to secure the future of his own church in Antioch').
settings.readers: The church at Philadelphia, asked to choose one of its deacons for a long journey to Syria

title: Philo, Rheus and the brothers in Troas
sum: Philo, a deacon from Cilicia, and Rheus Agathopus, who followed Ignatius from Syria, bear witness to the welcome the Philadelphians gave them; Ignatius prays that those who dishonored them may be redeemed (11:1). The brothers in Troas greet them. Ignatius writes 'by Burrhus', whom the Ephesians and Smyrnaeans sent with him, and says farewell 'in Christ Jesus, the hope we share' (11:2).

views.H: Lightfoot: the two men 'had followed in the track of Ignatius', welcomed by most at Philadelphia and snubbed by some, 'doubtless his Judaizing opponents'. They are also in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 10:1.
views.N: Troas is where Paul saw the man of Macedonia and broke bread on the first day of the week (Acts 16:8-11; Acts 20:6-12).

echoes: Acts 16:8-11; Acts 20:5-12; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 10:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer (not named), council of elders and deacons; Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Smyrna
settings.when: At Troas, after the stay at Smyrna, before sailing for Macedonia (11:2; Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10)
settings.why: To thank the church for welcoming his companions, to pray for those who had not, and to close with greetings from Troas.
settings.readers: The church, including both those who had welcomed Philo and Rheus Agathopus and those who had dishonored them (Lightfoot)
